claims.text: Al and Ti are low-density elements suitable for lightweight HEAs.
Rapid quenching or high-energy deposition can produce a homogeneous, chemically disordered single-phase, amorphous, or nanocrystalline structure in a lightweight HEA.
Conventional processing of the same composition produces a heterogeneous multiphase microstructure with compositional inhomogeneities and intermetallic precipitates.
High configurational entropy creates lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion and thereby increases mechanical strength.
A homogeneous, chemically disordered microstructure with lattice distortion promotes nucleation of a continuous, dense, adherent passive oxide film.
Chemical disorder and a homogeneous surface improve corrosion resistance.
A continuous passive oxide film protects the alloy against corrosion.
A continuous passive oxide film protects the alloy against high-temperature oxidation.
The homogeneous single-phase variant will have higher mechanical strength than the conventionally processed heterogeneous variant of the same composition.
The homogeneous single-phase variant will have a lower corrosion current density than the conventionally processed heterogeneous variant.
The homogeneous single-phase variant will have lower oxidation mass gain at approximately 900 °C than the conventionally processed heterogeneous variant.
The proposed structural state improves strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance while retaining low density.
Composition changes that favor segregation or phase separation can eliminate the proposed benefits.
Temperatures above the passive film's stability range can cause film breakdown and eliminate the corrosion and oxidation benefits.
The magnitude of improvements depends on processing details and precise alloy composition.
Failure of the homogeneous group to show statistically significant improvement in all three measured property classes would falsify the hypothesis.
